arXiv:2605.00360v1 [cs.LG] 01 May 2026

Binomial flows: Denoising and flow matching for discrete ordinal data

Yair Shenfeld Address: Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA 02912 Email address: yair_shenfeld@brown.edu , Ricardo Baptista Address: Department of Statistical Sciences, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada M5G 1X6 Email address: r.baptista@utoronto.ca and Stefano Peluchetti Address: Sakana AI, Tokyo, Japan Email address: stepelu@sakana.ai
Abstract.

Flow-based generative modeling in continuous spaces exploit Tweedie’s formula to express the denoiser (learned in training) as a score function (used in sampling). In contrast, this relation has been largely missing in the discrete setting where common approaches focus on learning discrete scores and rates. In this work we close this gap for discrete non-negative ordinal data by introducing Binomial flows. Our framework provides a simple recipe for training a discrete diffusion model which simultaneously denoises, samples, and estimates exact likelihoods. We verify our methodology on synthetic examples and obtain competitive results on real-world data sets.

1. Introduction

Flow matching and diffusion models in continuous spaces are currently state-of-the-art methods for the generation of images, video, audio, proteins, and robotic data LHH+ (24). Given that many of these structured dataset are naturally defined over discrete spaces, e.g., using 8-bit representations of images, text, molecules LNC+ (25), there is active research in bringing these flow-based models into the discrete setting. While many of the ideas of flow-based methods carry over from continuous to discrete settings, there are in fact some important differences and missing gaps. In continuous spaces, the standard approaches perturb data points with additive noise, train a denoiser to recover the clean data points from their noisy versions, and then sequentially apply denoising steps to sample new data points. A key relation for using denoisers to solve the sampling task correctly is Tweedie’s formula, which expresses the denoiser as the score function of the perturbed data distribution. The score is used to sample using a variety of iterative techniques, such as Langevin dynamics or time-reversed diffusion-based solvers, which progressively transform noise into samples from the target data distribution.

In contrast, flow-based methods in discrete spaces have mostly focused on learning a (discrete analogue of the) score. This is partly due to the fact that Gaussian noise, which is the natural choice for perturbing the data in continuous settings, satisfies a Tweedie’s formula relating denoisers and scores, while the analogue of Gaussian noise in the discrete setting is less clear. As argued in recent works PSO+ (25); KAAL (22); LH (25), learning denoisers, as opposed to scores, improves stability in training so it is of interest to find a discrete analogue to Tweedie’s formula. In this paper we show that when the data is defined over an ordered discrete space with nonnegative data, Binomial noise is the analogue of Gaussian noise. Based on this observation we introduce a simple recipe for training a discrete diffusion model which mirrors diffusion models in continuous spaces.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. (1)

    We show that choosing the noising distributions to be Binomial allows us to directly learn the denoiser, which in turn satisfies a discrete Tweedie’s formula.

  2. (2)

    We show that the discrete Tweedie’s formula yields exact samples from the data distribution in a finite time through the Poisson-Föllmer process.

  3. (3)

    We derive an identity for the likelihood of the data distribution involving the Binomial flow denoiser, which leads to exact likelihood estimation and training.

  4. (4)

    We validate our methodology on various synthetic and real-world datasets and obtain competitive FID values on imaging datasets.

In the remainder of the introduction, we review in more detail the general framework of flow matching and diffusion models. Section 2 presents our main results on the Binomial flows and the Poisson-Föllmer process. Section 3 describes our experiments. Section 4 covers the relevant related work. The proofs of our results and further information are contained in Appendices A-J.

1.1. Learning denoisers

Consider a data distribution μ\mu over an ordered space 𝒪\mathcal{O}, e.g, 𝒪=ℝd\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{R}^{d} or 𝒪=ℕd\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{N}^{d}. Our goal is to learn a denoiser

(1.1) m⁡(t,x):=𝔼⁡[XT|Xt=x]\mathrm{m}(t,x):=\mathbb{E}[X_{T}|X_{t}=x]

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and x∈𝒪x\in\mathcal{O}, where XtX_{t} is a noisy version of XT∼μX_{T}\sim\mu with tt standing for the signal level. A flow-based recipe to train a denoiser is to choose a family of conditional distributions pt|Tp_{t|T} on 𝒪\mathcal{O}, for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], such that

  1. (i)

    pt|T(⋅|xT)p_{t|T}(\cdot|x_{T}) can be easily sampled for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and xT∈𝒪x_{T}\in\mathcal{O},

  2. (ii)

    pT|T​(xT|y)=δy​(xT)p_{T|T}(x_{T}|y)=\delta_{y}(x_{T}) for all xT,y∈𝒪x_{T},y\in\mathcal{O},

  3. (iii)

    p0|T(⋅|xT)p_{0|T}(\cdot|x_{T}) is independent of xTx_{T} for all xT∈𝒪x_{T}\in\mathcal{O}.

Property (i) means that it is easy to perturb a data point xTx_{T}, property (ii) means that at time t=Tt=T, when there is no perturbation, xtx_{t} corresponds to the clean data. Property (iii) means that at t=0t=0 the data point xTx_{T} is forgotten and x0x_{0} is pure noise. Once the family (pt|T)t∈[0,T](p_{t|T})_{t\in[0,T]} is constructed, we define the flow (pt)t∈[0,T](p_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} of probability measures as

(1.2) pt​(xt):=∫𝒪pt|T​(xt|xT)​μ​(xT).p_{t}(x_{t}):=\int_{\mathcal{O}}p_{t|T}(x_{t}|x_{T})\mu(x_{T}).

By construction, pT=μp_{T}=\mu, and p0p_{0} is a measure which is independent of the data, typically assumed to be easy to sample. Thus, the flow (pt)t∈[0,T](p_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} interpolates between an easy distribution at t=0t=0 to the data distribution μ\mu at t=Tt=T. To learn the denoiser m\mathrm{m} in (1.1), with Xt∼ptX_{t}\sim p_{t}, we minimize

(1.3) minθ∫0T∫𝒪w(t)Dℓ(xT,mθ(t,xt))pt|T(xt|xT)μ(xT)dt,\min_{\theta}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{O}}w(t)\mathrm{D}_{\ell}\left(x_{T},\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(t,x_{t})\right)p_{t|T}(x_{t}|x_{T})\mu(x_{T})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t,

where Dℓ\mathrm{D}_{\ell} is a Bregman divergence for a convex function ℓ\ell (e.g., quadratic, entropic), w:[0,T]→ℝ+w\colon[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} is a time-dependent weight, and {mθ}θ\{\mathrm{m}_{\theta}\}_{\theta} is a class of functions parameterized by θ\theta. For example, with ℓ⁡(x)=|x|22\ell(x)=\frac{|x|^{2}}{2}, the optimization problem (1.3) reads

(1.4) minθ∫0T∫𝒪w(t)|xT−mθ(t,xt)|2pt|T(xt|xT)μ(xT)dt.\min_{\theta}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{O}}w(t)\left|x_{T}-\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(t,x_{t})\right|^{2}p_{t|T}(x_{t}|x_{T})\mu(x_{T})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

A standard computation BGW (05), BGB+ (25) shows that m⁡(t,x)=𝔼⁡[XT|Xt=x]\mathrm{m}(t,x)=\mathbb{E}[X_{T}|X_{t}=x] is the unique minimizer of (1.3) for any strictly convex ℓ\ell, provided that {mθ}θ\{\mathrm{m}_{\theta}\}_{\theta} is a sufficiently large class of functions. The advantage of the objective (1.3) is that, given i.i.d. samples from μ\mu, it can be estimated with Monte Carlo, since by property (i) sampling from pt|T(⋅|xT)p_{t|T}(\cdot|x_{T}) is easy.

1.2. Sampling with denoisers

In the context of generative modeling one is interested in using a denoiser mθ\mathrm{m}_{\theta} to generate new samples from μ\mu. In the continuous setting, e.g., 𝒪=ℝd\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, this can be achieved by choosing the conditional distributions to be Gaussian. For example, we can choose

(1.5) pt|T(⋅|xT):=𝒩(tTxT,t⁡(T−t)TId),p_{t|T}(\cdot|x_{T}):=\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{t}{T}x_{T},\frac{t(T-t)}{T}I_{d}\right),

which indeed satisfies (i)-(ii)-(iii)11 1 With the choice (1.5) we have p0|T(⋅|xT)=δ0p_{0|T}(\cdot|x_{T})=\delta_{0}, where other Gaussian models would lead to, for example, p0|T(⋅|xT)≈𝒩(0,Id)p_{0|T}(\cdot|x_{T})\approx\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). In our exposition we chose (1.5) to make the analogy with the discrete case clearer; cf. Appendix H.. In order to sample we use Tweedie’s formula,

(1.6) m(t,x)=Ttx+(T−t)∇logpt(x)\mathrm{m}(t,x)=\frac{T}{t}x+(T-t)\,\nabla\log p_{t}(x)

to express the denoiser m⁡(t,x)\mathrm{m}(t,x) in terms of the score ∇log⁡pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x). Once we have an estimate of ∇log⁡pt\nabla\log p_{t} we can sample from μ\mu via a number of methods such as time-reversal, (annealed) Langevin dynamics, and probability flows HJA (20); SSDK+ (21); SE (19).

The setting of discrete data posses a challenge to implementing the above approach, due to the lack of the Gaussian distribution, and the lack of ordinal structure. Instead, most approaches focus on learning the distributions pT|t(⋅|xt)p_{T|t}(\cdot|x_{t}), which predicts clean data from its noisy versions, and then use these distributions in sampling, often in heuristic ways. Since the denoiser m⁡(t,xt)\mathrm{m}(t,x_{t}) is simply the mean of pT|t(⋅|xt)p_{T|t}(\cdot|x_{t}), it is much easier to learn, so being able to get exact samples using just the denoiser is of great value. This is precisely the goal we achieve in this work.

2. Binomial flows

2.1. Binomial denoisers

Let xT∈ℕdx_{T}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} be a clean data point which we wish to noise into xt∈ℕdx_{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. In the continuous setting the natural and common approach is to use additive noise to perturb the data, xt=xT+(T−t)​yx_{t}=x_{T}+(T-t)y where yy is the noise. But in the discrete setting such perturbation will yield xt∉ℕdx_{t}\notin\mathbb{N}^{d}. Our approach is to use thinning as a substitute to addition. In particular, we thin xT∈ℕdx_{T}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} by sampling xt|xTx_{t}|x_{T} from a Binomial (product) distribution with the number of trials xTx_{T} and success probability tT\frac{t}{T}. Clearly, at t=Tt=T we recover the clean data xTx_{T}, while at t=0t=0 we have no signal left, x0=0x_{0}=0. We now make these definitions precise.

Let Binomialn,α\operatorname{Binomial}_{n,\alpha} be the binomial distribution with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} trials and probability of success α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1],

Binomialn,α(k)=(nk)αk(1−α)n−k,k=0,…,n.\operatorname{Binomial}_{n,\alpha}(k)={n\choose k}\alpha^{k}(1-\alpha)^{n-k},\quad k=0,\ldots,n.

For xT∈ℕdx_{T}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} let BinomialxT,α\operatorname{Binomial}_{x_{T},\alpha} stand for the product distribution that factorizes over each component

BinomialxT,α=∏i=1dBinomialxTi,α,xT=(xT1,…,xTd).\operatorname{Binomial}_{x_{T},\alpha}=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\operatorname{Binomial}_{x_{T}^{i},\alpha},\quad x_{T}=(x_{T}^{1},\ldots,x_{T}^{d}).

Given a data sample xT∈ℕdx_{T}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} we define the Binomial flow as the family of conditional distributions for the thinned data,

(2.1) pt|T​(xt|xT):=BinomialxT,tT⁡(xt).p_{t|T}(x_{t}|x_{T}):=\operatorname{Binomial}_{x_{T},\frac{t}{T}}(x_{t}).

We note that the choice (2.1) satisfies properties (i), (ii), (iii), with p0|T​(x0|xT)=δ0p_{0|T}(x_{0}|x_{T})=\delta_{0}. The denoiser is given by

(2.2) m(t,x):=𝔼XT∼pT|t(⋅|Xt=x)[XT|Xt=x],\mathrm{m}(t,x):=\mathbb{E}_{X_{T}\sim p_{T|t}(\cdot|X_{t}=x)}[X_{T}|X_{t}=x],

where pT|t(⋅|Xt)∝pt|T(Xt|⋅)μ(⋅)p_{T|t}(\cdot|X_{t})\propto p_{t|T}(X_{t}|\cdot)\mu(\cdot) and Xt|XT∼pt|T(⋅|XT)=BinomialXT,tTX_{t}|X_{T}\sim p_{t|T}(\cdot|X_{T})=\operatorname{Binomial}_{X_{T},\frac{t}{T}}. The denoiser m\mathrm{m} can be estimated by solving (1.3) for the Binomial flow as shown in Algorithm 1.

Once the denoiser in (2.2) is estimated we need to find a way to use it in sampling. In the following sections we will show that there exists a continuous time Markov chain (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} in ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}, the Poisson-Föllmer process, with intensity λ⁡(t,x)\lambda(t,x) such that

  1. (a)

    XT∼μ,X0=0X_{T}\sim\mu,\qquad X_{0}=0,

  2. (b)

    Xt|XT∼pt|T(⋅|XT)=BinomialXT,tTX_{t}|X_{T}\sim p_{t|T}(\cdot|X_{T})=\operatorname{Binomial}_{X_{T},\frac{t}{T}},

  3. (c)

    m⁡(t,Xt)−XtT−t=λ⁡(t,Xt)\frac{\mathrm{m}(t,X_{t})-X_{t}}{T-t}=\lambda(t,X_{t}).

The combination of (a)-(b)-(c) is the precise discrete analogue of the Gaussian setting. Property (a) guarantees that the process matches the data distribution at the final time t=Tt=T, property (b) allows us to estimate the denoiser m\mathrm{m} by solving (1.3), and property (c) is a discrete Tweedie’s formula, which shows how to use the denoiser to sample (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} via Algorithm 2.

In the next section we formally introduce the process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}. It will be shown to possess desirable theoretical properties, and in addition will yield an identity to compute the likelihood of the data under this process via a particular choice of a Bregman divergence.

2.2. The Poisson-Föllmer process

The Poisson-Föllmer process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} is a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) with values in ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}. We refer to (CBB+, 22) for a quick introduction to CTMC in the context of discrete diffusion models, and recall that the rate matrix Rt​(x,y)x,y∈𝒪R_{t}(x,y)_{x,y\in\mathcal{O}} completely describes the process. The rate matrix for the Poisson-Föllmer process is

(2.3) Rt​(x,y)={λi​(t,x)if ​y=x+ei,1−∑i=1dλi​(t,x)if ​y=x,0else,R_{t}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\lambda^{i}(t,x)&\textnormal{if }y=x+e_{i},\\ 1-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda^{i}(t,x)&\textnormal{if }y=x,\\ 0&\textnormal{else},\end{cases}

where {ei}i=1d\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} are the one-hot vectors and {λi​(t,x)}i=1d\{\lambda^{i}(t,x)\}_{i=1}^{d} are the intensities defined below. In words, The Poisson-Föllmer process (Xt)(X_{t}) is a continuous-time counting-process where at time tt each coordinate XtiX_{t}^{i} jumps up to Xti+1X_{t}^{i}+1 with intensity λi​(t,Xt)\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t}). Note that the decision of each coordinate to jump depends on the current values of all the other coordinates since the intensity λi​(t,Xt)\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t}) of the iith coordinate depends on XtX_{t}, rather than just XtiX_{t}^{i}. The intensities will be chosen in such a way that we are guaranteed that XTX_{T} is distributed like the data distribution μ\mu.

To define the intensity

(2.4) λ⁡(t,x):=(λ1​(t,x),…,λd​(t,x)),\lambda(t,x):=(\lambda^{1}(t,x),\ldots,\lambda^{d}(t,x)),

we start with the definition of the one-dimensional Poisson distribution πt\pi_{t} with parameter t≥0t\geq 0,

(2.5) πt​(k)=e−t​tkk!,k∈ℕ,\pi_{t}(k)=e^{-t}\frac{t^{k}}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb{N},

and its multi-dimensional extension,

(2.6) πt​(x)=∏j=1dπt​(xj),x=(x1,…,xd)∈ℕd.\pi_{t}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\pi_{t}(x^{j}),\qquad x=(x^{1},\ldots,x^{d})\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.

Based on the Poisson distribution we define the Poisson semigroup (which is analogous to the convolution operator/heat semigroup defined by the Gaussian distribution).

Definition 2.1 (The Poisson semigroup).

Let G:ℕd→ℝG:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be such that ∑x∈ℕd|G⁡(x)|​πt​(x)<+∞\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}|G(x)|\pi_{t}(x)<+\infty. The Poisson semigroup (Pt)t≥0(\mathrm{P}_{t})_{t\geq 0} is given by

(2.7) Pt​G​(x):=∑y∈ℕdG⁡(x+y)​πt​(y).\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x+y)\pi_{t}(y).

The intensities are now defined by

(2.8) λi​(t,x):=PT−t​f​(x+ei)PT−t​f​(x),t∈[0,T],x∈ℕd,\lambda^{i}(t,x):=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{T-t}f(x+e_{i})}{\mathrm{P}_{T-t}f(x)},\quad t\in[0,T],\quad x\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

where {ei}i=1d\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} are the one-hot vectors, and where ff is the ratio of the data distribution μ\mu and πT\pi_{T},

(2.9) f⁡(x):=μ⁡(x)πT​(x),x∈ℕd.f(x):=\frac{\mu(x)}{\pi_{T}(x)},\qquad x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.

Once the intensities are defined as in Equation 2.8 one can verify that XTX_{T} follows the data distribution μ\mu (Corollary D.2). The form of the intensities in (2.8) is the discrete analogue of the score in the continuous setting (Appendix H), and similarly cannot be computed simply from the definition (2.8). However, in the next section we will overcome this issue using our discrete Tweedie’s formula.

2.3. Binomial denoisers and the Poisson-Föllmer process

Our first key result is that learning the Binomial denoiser allows us to sample the data distribution using the Poisson-Föllmer process.

Proposition 2.2.

Fix T>0T>0 and let μ=f​πT\mu=f\pi_{T}, with f:ℕd→(0,∞)f:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to(0,\infty) bounded from above and below by positive constants22 2 These assumptions are innocuous in practice as positivity can be guaranteed by setting the probability of any specific x∈ℕdx\in\mathbb{N}^{d} to be arbitrarily small, while the upper bound assumption can be guaranteed with a large enough upper bound., be a distribution on ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}. The Poisson-Föllmer process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} with the intensities (2.8) satisfies (a)-(b)-(c),

  1. (a)

    XT∼μ,X0=0X_{T}\sim\mu,\qquad X_{0}=0,

  2. (b)

    Xt|XT∼pt|T(⋅|XT)=BinomialXT,tTX_{t}|X_{T}\sim p_{t|T}(\cdot|X_{T})=\operatorname{Binomial}_{X_{T},\frac{t}{T}},

  3. (c)

    m⁡(t,Xt)−XtT−t=λ⁡(t,Xt)\frac{\mathrm{m}(t,X_{t})-X_{t}}{T-t}=\lambda(t,X_{t}).

In light of Proposition 2.2 we can now combine Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 to sample from the data distribution. Algorithm 1 trains the denoiser m\mathrm{m} using Binomial thinning (b), and given the trained denoiser m\mathrm{m}, Algorithm 2 leverages the discrete Tweedie’s formula (c) to get samples from the data distribution μ\mu (a).

The next result shows that once the intensity λ\lambda is estimated we automatically get exact likelihood estimates. Alternatively, the identity below can be used to train the denoiser via maximum likelihood.

Proposition 2.3 (Likelihood estimation).

Let λ\lambda be the intensity defined by (2.4)-(2.8). Then,

(2.10) −log⁡μ⁡(x)=∫0T𝔼y∼Binomialx,t​[Dℓ​(x−yT−t,λ⁡(t,y))]​⁡𝑑t,-\log\mu(x)=\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,t}}\left[\mathrm{D}_{\ell}\left(\frac{x-y}{T-t},\lambda(t,y)\right)\right]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t,

where, for a∈ℕda\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

(2.11) ℓ⁡(a)=∑i=1dai​log⁡ai,∇ℓ​(a):=(1+log⁡a1,…,1+log⁡ad),\ell(a)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}a^{i}\log a^{i},\quad\nabla\ell(a):=(1+\log a^{1},\ldots,1+\log a^{d}),

and, for a,b∈ℕda,b\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

(2.12) Dℓ​(a,b):=ℓ⁡(a)−ℓ⁡(b)−∇ℓ​(b)⋅(a−b)=∑i=1d[ai​log⁡ai−ai​log⁡bi−ai+bi].\begin{split}\mathrm{D}_{\ell}(a,b)&:=\ell(a)-\ell(b)-\nabla\ell(b)\cdot(a-b)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[a^{i}\log a^{i}-a^{i}\log b^{i}-a^{i}+b^{i}\right].\end{split}

2.4. The many facets of the Poisson-Föllmer process

The previous sections described the Poisson-Föllmer process by explicitly defining its rate matrix. In this section we provide equivalent descriptions of the process which, while interesting theoretically, are not needed for the implementation of our Binomial flow discrete diffusion model.

The first description goes through the notion of a controlled Poisson point process. This description is made rigorous in Appendix C, and here we will provide the rough idea which is portrayed in Figure 1. We begin with dd independent Poisson point processes in [0,T]×[0,C][0,T]\times[0,C] (for large enough constant CC), and dd curves (λti)t∈[0,T](\lambda^{i}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} for i=1,…,di=1,\ldots,d. The iith coordinate (Xti)t∈[0,T](X_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]} of (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} is a non-decreasing process in ℕ\mathbb{N}, starting at X0i=0X_{0}^{i}=0, whose value at time tt is equal to the number of points from the iith Poisson point process that fall in the region under the curves λi\lambda^{i} by time tt. Each of the curve λi\lambda^{i} is chosen stochastically, depending on the values of all the coordinates of (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}. These curves can be chosen to guarantee that at time TT the process follows the data distribution, XT∼μX_{T}\sim\mu.

The second description is that of a Schrödinger bridge or Doob hh-transform. In Appendix F we show that the Poisson-Föllmer process is a special case of a Schrödinger bridge: Of all processes starting at 0 whose distribution at time TT is the data distribution μ\mu, the Poisson-Föllmer process is the closest to a dd-dimensional Poisson process. Alternatively, it can be described as a Doob hh-transform, where a standard Poisson process in ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d} is conditioned to be distributed like the data distribution μ\mu at time TT (rather than πT\pi_{T}); see L1́ (4). The connection between the Poisson-Föllmer process and the Doob hh-transform goes through

(2.13) λi(t,x)=h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x),i=1,…,d,\lambda^{i}(t,x)=\frac{h(t,x+e_{i})}{h(t,x)},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d,

where the hh-transform is given by h⁡(t,x)=PT−t​f​(x)h(t,x)=\mathrm{P}_{T-t}f(x).

The third description is that of time reversal. Define the forward process Z→t:=XT−t\vec{Z}_{t}:=X_{T-t} to be a Poisson bridge which starts at Z→0∼μ\vec{Z}_{0}\sim\mu and terminates at Z→T=0\vec{Z}_{T}=0. Then, the Poisson-Föllmer process Xt=:Zt→X_{t}=:\reflectbox{$\vec{\reflectbox{$Z_{t}$}}$} is the reverse process obtained by the time-reversal of Z→t\vec{Z}_{t}. Hence, from the perspective of the time-reversal approach in discrete diffusions LME (24), our goal should be learn the discrete score [qt​(y)qt​(x)]y≠x\left[\frac{q_{t}(y)}{q_{t}(x)}\right]_{y\neq x}, where qtq_{t} is the distribution of Z→t\vec{Z}_{t}. In Appendix G we show that this task is equivalent to the task of learning the intensity λ\lambda.

Remark 2.4 (Gaussian analogues: The Föllmer process).

The Poisson-Föllmer process has a continuous analogue, the Föllmer process, which shares many of its properties, as we explain in Appendix H. As the Poisson-Föllmer process, the Föllmer process starts at a deterministic point, in contrast to most diffusion models which begin at a Gaussian distribution.

3. Numerical experiments

In this section we present our results from training a denoiser given samples from a discrete target distribution μ\mu, to generate new samples from μ\mu. Section 3.1 presents the results on synthetic datasets, while Section 3.2 evaluates our method on the CIFAR-10 dataset. In all of our experiments we learn the denoiser mθ\mathrm{m}_{\theta} by minimizing the weighted squared error loss

(3.1) minθ∫0T∫𝒪w(t)|xT−mθ(t,xt)|2pt|T(xt|xT)μ(xT)dt\min_{\theta}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{O}}w(t)\left|x_{T}-\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(t,x_{t})\right|^{2}p_{t|T}(x_{t}|x_{T})\mu(x_{T})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t

over an appropriate class of neural networks. After learning the denoiser, we define the rate function as λθ​(t,xt)=mθ​(xt,t)−xtT−t.\lambda_{\theta}(t,x_{t})=\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)-x_{t}}{T-t}. We use the rate to generate new samples using Algorithm 2 with either an Euler or τ−\tau-leaping method as in Algorithms 3 or 4, respectively. In the following experiments we choose T=1T=1.

3.1. Synthetic data

In this section we apply our approach to various d=1d=1-dimensional synthetic distributions for non-negative ordinal data that are considered in BGB+ (25). These distributions are selected to display characteristics such as bimodality and heavy tails. The definition of each distribution and details on the model architecture and training of the denoiser for this experiment can found in Appendix I.

We learn the model parameters by minimizing the loss (3.1) with uniform time-sampling and weight w⁡(t)=(1−t)−0.5,w(t)=(1-t)^{-0.5}, which encourages the model to more accurately approximate the true denoiser near the data distribution at t=1t=1. We learn the denoiser using 50,000 i.i.d. samples x1x_{1} from the data distribution and generate 10,00010,000 i.i.d. samples from the learned model using an Euler sampler (Algorithm 3) with 1000 time-steps.

True samples and generated samples from the predicted distributions are plotted in Figure 2, showing that Binomial flows closely captures both bimodal features, heavy tails and distributions with varying support.

For each distribution, we also evaluate the performance quantitatively. We use the likelihood identity in (2.10) to evaluate the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the true samples under the predicted distribution. We use a Monte Carlo estimator with 10001000 samples to evaluate the NLL for each data sample x1∼μx_{1}\sim\mu and compute the average NLL over 10,00010,000 data samples. Table 1 reports the average and standard error of the NLL over five training instances. For most examples, we observe close agreement to the true NLL evaluated by using the exact evaluations of the target distribution. Table 3 in Appendix I also compares the W1W_{1} distance between the generated and true data samples to the results presented in (BGB+, 25). For the ZIP, Zipf and Yule-Simon distributions we observe statistically significant closer results to the target with Binomial flows.

3.2. CIFAR-10

We evaluate our method on the CIFAR-10 dataset using the EDM framework (KAAL, 22). We adopt the DDPM++ architecture (SSDK+, 21) for the denoiser, data pipeline, training loop, and FID computation from the EDM codebase without modification. The following subsections provide some information on our training and sampling for CIFAR-10, and we refer to Appendix J for more information.

3.2.1. Preconditioning and Training

We adapt EDM’s preconditioning strategy to the Binomial flow setting. We emphasize that this is possible due to our ability to work with the quadratic loss (3.1). We parametrize the denoiser as

(3.2) mθ​(xt,t)=cskip​(t)​xt+cout​(t)​Fθ​(cin​(t)​xt+sin,t),\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)=c_{\textnormal{skip}}(t)x_{t}+c_{\textnormal{out}}(t)F_{\theta}(c_{\text{in}}(t)x_{t}+s_{\text{in}},t),

with a neural network FθF_{\theta}, where the parameters cskip​(t),cout​(t),cin​(t),sinc_{\textnormal{skip}}(t),c_{\textnormal{out}}(t),c_{\text{in}}(t),s_{\text{in}} are chosen in a way which stabilizes training. We provide more details in Section J.1 and summarize the parameters in Table 4.

3.2.2. Time Parameterization

We parameterize time using the noise level σ=−log⁡(t+εnoise)\sigma=-\log(t+\varepsilon_{\text{noise}}) for εnoise=10−5\varepsilon_{\text{noise}}=10^{-5}, which is provided to the neural network as the time argument. This logarithmic parameterization is crucial for the Binomial flow, as it provides appropriate resolution near t≈0t\approx 0 where the signal-to-noise ratio changes rapidly. Figure 3 illustrates the denoiser’s behavior at t=0.001t=0.001. Even though xtx_{t} appears nearly indistinguishable from noise and t≈0t\approx 0, the denoiser already reconstructs the overall long-range structure of the image. This should be compared with the case t=0t=0, where 𝔼⁡[X1|X0]=𝔼⁡[X1]\mathbb{E}[X_{1}|X_{0}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]. Additional denoiser plots are shown in Section J.2.

Figure 4 demonstrates that uniform discretization in noise space σ\sigma yields a more natural progression of the generative process compared to uniform discretization in time tt.

3.2.3. Noise Sampling

To design an effective noise sampling strategy for training, we analyze where the learned denoiser improves over a simple baseline. We first derive the optimal affine baseline b⁡(t):=bskip​(t)​Xt+bout​(t)​μdata\mathrm{b}(t):=b_{\text{skip}}(t)X_{t}+b_{\text{out}}(t)\mu_{\text{data}} that minimizes the expected squared error 𝖫t​(b)=𝔼⁡[|X1−b⁡(t)|2]\mathsf{L}_{t}(\mathrm{b})=\mathbb{E}[|X_{1}-\mathrm{b}(t)|^{2}] at each time tt; see Claim J.6. We plot the time evolution of all scaling coefficients in Section J.2.

Given a trained denoiser m\mathrm{m} we compute the improvement 𝖫σ​(b)−𝖫σ​(m)\mathsf{L}_{\sigma}(\mathrm{b})-\mathsf{L}_{\sigma}(\mathrm{m}) as a function of the noise level σ\sigma. This quantity measures how much the neural network improves over the baseline at each noise level and thus indicates which noise levels contribute most to learning. As shown in Figure 7, the normalized improvement curve is well-approximated by a Gaussian distribution in σ\sigma-space. This observation motivates sampling noise levels from a truncated Gaussian σ∼𝒩⁡(μσ,γσ2)​𝟏[0,−log⁡(εnoise)]​(σ)\sigma\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\sigma},\gamma^{2}_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}_{[0,-\log(\varepsilon_{\text{noise}})]}(\sigma) during training, with μσ\mu_{\sigma} and γσ\gamma_{\sigma} chosen to match the empirical improvement curve. Figure 7 compares this distribution to uniform sampling in time (t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]), showing that the Gaussian strategy allocates more training budget to noise levels where improvement is achievable.

3.2.4. Results

Figure 5 shows unconditional samples from our model, demonstrating diverse and realistic image generation. We generate samples using the τ\tau-leaping sampler (Algorithm 4) with 1024 uniformly-spaced time steps. While this number of function evaluations (NFE) is higher than state-of-the-art continuous diffusion models (e.g., EDM achieves lower FID with only 36 NFE), it is consistent with discrete diffusion methods (GRS+, 24; CSL+, 25) and earlier continuous models (SSDK+, 21). The denoising trajectories in Figure 4 suggest room for improved time discretization schedules, which we leave to future work. Table 2 summarizes quantitative comparisons against both continuous and discrete diffusion baselines.

Our Binomial Flow approach achieves an FID of 2.94, demonstrating highly competitive performance. Notably, while continuous models operating on real-valued data achieve slightly better scores, our method outperforms the other discrete diffusion baselines.

4. Related work

In the continuous setting, diffusion models were gradually developed over the recent decade HJA (20); SSDK+ (21). Later, a flow-matching perspective was developed in the concurrent works LCBH+ (23); AVE (23); LGql (23). Discrete diffusions in discrete time were systematically considered in AJH+ (21), though their origin can be found in HNJ+ (21) and SME (21). The first paper to introduce discrete diffusions in continuous time as Continuous Time Markov Chains is CBB+ (22). Mirroring the historical developments of diffusion models in continuous spaces, the early versions of discrete diffusions were trained using cross-entropy and evidence lower bound (ELBO) based objectives. The first paper to consider a (discrete) score based approach was LME (24), and a flow matching perspective was given in CYB+ (24) and GRS+ (24).

The above approaches focus on learning the discrete score or the rate (analogous to velocity in the continuous setting), but not the denoiser (which is not a well-defined object in general discrete spaces). For binary data, e.g., 𝒪={0,1}d\mathcal{O}=\{0,1\}^{d}, BS (25); PSO+ (25) built a framework that learns both a denoiser and a discrete score. For nonnegative ordered data, as in our case, CZ (23); BGB+ (25); Mon (23) learn both a denoiser and a rate via a discrete Tweedie’s formula, but a key difference is that the conditional distributions in these works are Poisson, pt|T(⋅|xT)=Poissont​xTp_{t|T}(\cdot|x_{T})=\operatorname{Poisson}_{tx_{T}}, rather than Binomial as in our work. These two types of perturbations are of different nature. For example, the Binomial perturbation recovers the clean data at t=Tt=T, while the Poisson perturbation only does so in limit T→∞T\to\infty. Additionally, the Binomial perturbation is one-sided since Xt|XTX_{t}|X_{T} is guaranteed to be smaller than XTX_{T}, unlike the Poisson perturbation which can “overshoot" the effective support of the data. Finally, the Binomial perturbation leads to a sampling process, namely the Poisson-Föllmer process, with desirable properties; cf. Section 2.4. We note that BGB+ (25) inspired us to find our exact likelihood formula (2.10). Overall, it remains interesting to better understand the advantages and disadvantages of the Binomial vs. Poisson perturbations. Closest to approach is (SFLL, 23) which uses Binomial thinning as we do, but lacks the discrete Tweedie’s formula, and hence the connection to the Poisson-Föllmer process. The lack of the discrete Tweedie’s formula leads (SFLL, 23) to rely on a likelihood-base loss while our general framework allows for all Bregman divergences, which in turns lets us mirror the EDM framework (KAAL, 22).

The origin of the Poisson-Föllmer process can be found in BDM (11), but the explicit construction described in Section 2.2 was first given in dimension d=1d=1 in KL (19). More generally, a Poisson processes perspective on discrete diffusion models can be found in RCRY (25) and PSO+ (25). Both the Poisson-Föllmer, and its Gaussian analogue the Föllmer process, are special cases of Schrödinger bridges L1́ (4). In the context of generative modeling, the question of learning Schrödinger bridges in the continuous setting was taken by a number of works TR (19); BTHD (21); Pel (23); SBCD (23); CGH+ (24), and in the discrete setting by KKM+ (25); KK (25).

Conclusions and outlook

This work introduces Binomial flows as an analogue of Gaussian-based denoising for discrete diffusion models with non-negative ordinal data. The flows are defined by a denoiser, which can be expressed as the rate function for a Poisson-Föllmer process. Moreover, we show the denoiser can be learned by minimizing a mean-squared error loss given target data, and it provides exact likelihood estimation. While our framework obtains low FID values on the CIFAR-10 dataset, we observed higher sensitivity of FID to the classifier-free guidance (CFG) parameter for generation on the ImageNet dataset (with FID values around ten). In the future, it is of interest to study the interaction of our denoiser with CFG and identify optimal sampling parameters (e.g., time schedules for τ\tau-leaping) that minimize the computational cost of inference with our method. Finally, it will be interesting to investigate whether the martingale property of the denoiser 𝔼⁡[m⁡(t,Xt)|Xs]=m⁡(s,Xs)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{m}(t,X_{t})|X_{s}]=\mathrm{m}(s,X_{s}) can be used to improve traningin as in DDDD (23).

Content of Appendices

Appendix A covers some preliminaries on discrete calculus and the Poisson semigroup. Appendix B explains how to construct counting processes out of Poisson point processes, and Appendix C builds on these ideas to construct the Poisson-Föllmer process. Appendix D derives the forward and backward Kolmogorov equations for the Poisson-Föllmer process. In Appendix E we use this preliminary work to complete the proofs of Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 2.3. In Appendix F we explain the connection between the Poisson-Föllmer process and Schrödinger bridges, and in Appendix G we explain the connection to time-reversal. Appendix H reviews the analogous construction of the Poisson-Föllmer process in the continuous setting. Appendix I and Appendix J contain additional information about the experiments with synthetic and imaging data, respectively.

Appendix A The Poisson semigroup

We begin in Section A.1 by establishing our notation and by covering some preliminaries in discrete calculus. We then define the Poisson semigroup in Section A.2 and derive some of its basic properties.

A.2. The Poisson semigroup

We begin by recalling the definition of the Poisson distribution πt\pi_{t} with parameter t≥0t\geq 0, and its multi-dimensional extension,

(A.6) πt​(k)=e−t​tkk!,k∈ℕ,πt​(x)=∏i=1dπt​(xi),x=(x1,…,xd)∈ℕd.\pi_{t}(k)=e^{-t}\frac{t^{k}}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb{N},\qquad\pi_{t}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\pi_{t}(x^{i}),\qquad x=(x^{1},\ldots,x^{d})\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.

The Poisson distribution πt\pi_{t} satisfies the analogue of the heat equation for the Gaussian distribution.

Lemma A.2 (Poisson heat equation).

Let πt\pi_{t} be as in (A.6) and extend it ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} by setting πt​(x)=0\pi_{t}(x)=0 for x∈ℤd\ℕdx\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\backslash\mathbb{N}^{d}. Then, for t≥0t\geq 0 and x∈ℕdx\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

(A.7) ∂tπt(x)=−∑i=1d∂iπt(x−ei).\partial_{t}\pi_{t}(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}\pi_{t}(x-e_{i}).
Proof.

We use the convention k!=0k!=0 for k<0k<0. Then,

(A.8) ∂tπt​(x)πt​(x)=∂tlog⁡πt​(x)=∂t[∑i=1dlog⁡πt​(xi)]=∂t[∑i=1dlog⁡(e−t​txixi!)]=∑i=1d∂t[−t+xi​log​t−log⁡(xi!)]=∑i=1d[−1+xit],\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\partial_{t}\pi_{t}(x)}{\pi_{t}(x)}&=\partial_{t}\log\pi_{t}(x)=\partial_{t}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\pi_{t}(x^{i})\right]=\partial_{t}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\left(\frac{e^{-t}t^{x^{i}}}{x^{i}!}\right)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{t}\left[-t+x^{i}\log t-\log(x^{i}!)\right]\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[-1+\frac{x^{i}}{t}\right],\end{split}

so

(A.9) ∂tπt​(x)=−d​πt​(x)+∑i=1dxit​e−t​txixi!​∏l≠ie−t​txlxl!=−d​πt​(x)+∑i=1de−t​txi−1(xi−1)!​∏l≠ie−t​txlxl!=−d​πt​(x)+∑i=1dπt​(x−ei)=∑i=1d[πt(x−ei)−πt(x)]=−∑i=1d∂iπt(x−ei).\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}\pi_{t}(x)&=-d\,\pi_{t}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{x^{i}}{t}\frac{e^{-t}t^{x^{i}}}{x^{i}!}\prod_{l\neq i}\frac{e^{-t}t^{x^{l}}}{x^{l}!}=-d\,\pi_{t}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{e^{-t}t^{x^{i-1}}}{(x^{i}-1)!}\prod_{l\neq i}\frac{e^{-t}t^{x^{l}}}{x^{l}!}=-d\,\pi_{t}(x)+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\pi_{t}(x-e_{i})\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\pi_{t}(x-e_{i})-\pi_{t}(x)\right]=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}\pi_{t}(x-e_{i}).\end{split}

∎

In analogy with the heat semigroup defined by a convolution with a Gaussian distribution, one can define the Poisson semigroup defined by a discrete convolution with a Poisson distribution. Let G:ℕd→ℝG:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be such that ∑x∈ℕd|G⁡(x)|​πt​(x)<+∞\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}|G(x)|\pi_{t}(x)<+\infty. The Poisson semigroup (Pt)t≥0(\mathrm{P}_{t})_{t\geq 0} acts on GG according to

(A.10) Pt​G​(x):=∑y∈ℕdG⁡(x+y)​πt​(y).\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x):=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x+y)\pi_{t}(y).

The next result shows that the Poisson semigroup satisfies the Poisson heat equation.

Lemma A.3 (Poisson semigroup equation).

Let G:ℕd→ℝG:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be such that ∑x∈ℕd|G⁡(x)|​πt​(x)<+∞\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}|G(x)|\pi_{t}(x)<+\infty. Then,

(A.11) ∂tPt​G​(x)=∑i=1d∂iPt​G​(x).\partial_{t}\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x).
Proof.
(A.12) ∂tPt​G​(x)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x) =∂t∑y∈ℕdG⁡(x+y)​πt​(y)​=(A.7)−∑y∈ℕdG⁡(x+y)​∑i=1d∂iπt​(y−ei)\displaystyle=\partial_{t}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x+y)\pi_{t}(y)\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:Poisson_pde]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:Poisson_pde}\/)}}}}{=}-\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x+y)\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}\pi_{t}(y-e_{i})
(A.13) =(A.2)​∑i=1d∑y∈ℕd∂iG⁡(x+y)​πt​(y)=∑i=1d∂iPt​G​(x).\displaystyle\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:sum_by_parts]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:sum_by_parts}\/)}}}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\partial_{i}G(x+y)\pi_{t}(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}\mathrm{P}_{t}G(x).

∎

Appendix B Controlled Poisson point processes

We begin this section by defining a particular case of Poisson point processes. We then explain how such processes can be controlled via stochastic intensities to construct general counting processes on ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}. We conclude by reviewing some preliminaries of stochastic calculus in Poisson space.

Let T>0T>0, C>0C>0, and let 𝕏:=[0,T]×[0,C]\mathbb{X}:=[0,T]\times[0,C]. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the sigma-algebra generated by the Borel sets of 𝕏\mathbb{X} endowed with the product topology, and let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the Lebesgue measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Define the Poisson space (Ωi,ℱi,ℙi)(\Omega^{i},\mathcal{F}^{i},\mathbb{P}^{i}) over (𝕏,𝒳,ℒ)(\mathbb{X},\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) as the space of atomic measures, each of which has countably many atoms,

(B.1) Ωi:={ωi:ωi=∑jδ(tj,zj),(tj,zj)∈{} (at most countable)},\Omega^{i}:=\left\{\omega^{i}:\omega^{i}=\sum_{j}\delta_{(t_{j},z_{j})},\quad(t_{j},z_{j})\in\Set{\quad}\textnormal{ (at most countable)}\right\},

the sigma-algebra ℱi\mathcal{F}^{i} is generated by the set of functions ωi↦ωi​(A)\omega^{i}\mapsto\omega^{i}(A), for any fixed A∈𝒳A\in\mathcal{X},

(B.2) ℱi:=σ(Ωi∋ωi↦ωi(A):A∈𝒳),\mathcal{F}^{i}:=\sigma\left(\Omega^{i}\ni\omega^{i}\mapsto\omega^{i}(A):A\in\mathcal{X}\right),

and the probability measure ℙi\mathbb{P}^{i} is defined by the requirements

(B.3) ∀A∈𝒳,∀k∈ℕ,ℙi[{ωi∈Ωi:ωi(A)=k}]=πℒ⁡(A)(k),∀k∈ℕ,ωi​(A1),…,ωi​(Ak)​ are ℙi-independent if A1,…,Ak∈𝒳 are disjoint.\begin{split}&\forall~A\in\mathcal{X},~\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\quad\mathbb{P}^{i}[\{\omega^{i}\in\Omega^{i}:\omega^{i}(A)=k\}]=\pi_{\mathcal{L}(A)}(k),\\ &\forall~k\in\mathbb{N},\quad\omega^{i}(A_{1}),\ldots,\omega^{i}(A_{k})\textnormal{ are $\mathbb{P}^{i}$-independent if $A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}\in\mathcal{X}$ are disjoint}.\\ \end{split}

In words, under ℙi\mathbb{P}^{i}, the number of points that fall in disjoint regions are independent, and the number of points that fall in a region AA is distributed like a Poisson whose parameter is the Lebesgue volume of AA. We now define the space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ):=⨂i=1d(Ωi,ℱi,ℙi)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}):=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{d}(\Omega^{i},\mathcal{F}^{i},\mathbb{P}^{i}) to be the product space of the Poisson spaces {(Ωi,ℱi,ℙi)}i=1d\{(\Omega^{i},\mathcal{F}^{i},\mathbb{P}^{i})\}_{i=1}^{d}. Note that, by construction,

(B.4) ∀A1,…,Ad∈𝒳,ω1​(A1),…,ωd​(Ad)​ are ℙ-independent.\forall~A_{1},\ldots,A_{d}\in\mathcal{X},\quad\omega^{1}(A_{1}),\ldots,\omega^{d}(A_{d})\textnormal{ are $\mathbb{P}$-independent}.

The space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) is the analogue of the Wiener space with Wiener measure under which continuous functions [0,T]→ℝd[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{d} are standard dd-dimensional Brownian motions.

Given t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] let 𝒳t\mathcal{X}_{t} be the sigma-algebra generated by the Borel sets of [0,t]×[0,C][0,t]\times[0,C], and let

(B.5) ℱt:=σ(Ω∋ω↦ω(A):A∈𝒳t).\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma\left(\Omega\ni\omega\mapsto\omega(A):A\in\mathcal{X}_{t}\right).

In the continuous setting one works with stochastic differential equations which are generated by taking a Brownian motion and adding a drift and/or multiplying by diffusion matrix. In the discrete setting this role is taken by stochastic intensities. These are dd-dimensional stochastic processes λ=(λt1​…,λtd):Ω→ℝd\lambda=(\lambda^{1}_{t}\ldots,\lambda^{d}_{t}):\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d} which are predictable, i.e., the function [0,T]×Ω∋(t,ω)↦λt​(ω)[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,\omega)\mapsto\lambda_{t}(\omega) is measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra σ({(s,t]×A:s≤t≤T,A∈𝒳s})\sigma\left(\{(s,t]\times A:s\leq t\leq T,A\in\mathcal{X}_{s}\}\right).

We now show how to generate a counting process using an intensity λ\lambda. Suppose λ\lambda is an intensity such that ℙ\mathbb{P}-almost-surely |λti|≤C|\lambda^{i}_{t}|\leq C for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and all i∈[d]i\in[d]. We define the counting process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} by

(B.6) Xti(ω):=ωi({(s,z)∈{:}s<t,z<λsi(ω)}),X_{t}^{i}(\omega):=\omega^{i}\left(\{(s,z)\in\Set{:}s<t,z<\lambda_{s}^{i}(\omega)\}\right),

where Xt=(Xt1,…,Xtd)∈ℕdX_{t}=(X_{t}^{1},\ldots,X_{t}^{d})\in\mathbb{N}^{d}. In words, the value of XtiX_{t}^{i} is the number of points in ωi\omega^{i} in [0,t]×[0,C][0,t]\times[0,C] which fall under the curve (λsi)s∈[0,t](\lambda_{s}^{i})_{s\in[0,t]}; see Figure 1.

By construction, each of the coordinates (Xti)t∈[0,T](X_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]} is a process adapted to the filtration (ℱt)t∈[0,T](\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}, non-decreasing, integer-valued, and left-continuous. Further, since, with probability 1, each ωi\omega^{i} has only finitely many atoms in [0,t]×[0,C][0,t]\times[0,C], and no two atoms lie on the same vertical line {t}×[0,C]\{t\}\times[0,C], we get that (Xti)t∈[0,T](X_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]} has finitely many jumps, each of size 1. Note that the coordinates of XtX_{t} need not be independent (and indeed in our case they will generally be dependent), since the value of each XtiX_{t}^{i} is determined by (λsi)s∈[0,t](\lambda_{s}^{i})_{s\in[0,t]}, and the processes {(λti)t∈[0,T]}i=1d\{(\lambda_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]}\}_{i=1}^{d} can be dependent. (The analogy in the continuous setting is that although the coordinates of a standard Brownian motion are independent, the coordinates of a stochastic differential equation built on this Brownian motion will generally be dependent.) However, with probability 1, no two coordinates (Xti)t∈[0,T](X_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]} and (Xtj)t∈[0,T](X_{t}^{j})_{t\in[0,T]} will jump at the same time tt since there is zero probability for atoms coming from ωi\omega^{i} and ωj\omega^{j} to lie on the same vertical line {t}×[0,C]\{t\}\times[0,C].

The next result is the discrete analogue of the Itô formula for counting processes. This is a classical result (e.g, p. 16 in [21]), so we will only sketch its proof. To explain the result we first need to explain the discrete analogue of a “stochastic integral", which is in fact much simpler in the discrete setting and can be defined pathwise. The stochastic integral ∫st⋅dXri(ω)\int_{s}^{t}\cdot\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i}(\omega) is the usual Riemann-Stieltjes integral given by, for a function H:[0,T]→ℝH:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R},

(B.7) ∫stHr​⁡d​Xri​(ω):=∑s≤rj≤tHrji,\int_{s}^{t}H_{r}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i}(\omega):=\sum_{s\leq r_{j}\leq t}H_{r_{j}^{i}},

where {rji}j\{r_{j}^{i}\}_{j} are the jump times of (Xri​(ω))r∈[0,T](X_{r}^{i}(\omega))_{r\in[0,T]} between ss and tt.

Lemma B.1 (Discrete Itô formula).

Let G:[0,T]×ℕd→ℝG:[0,T]\times\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a function which is differentiable in tt. Then, ℙ\mathbb{P}-almost-surely,

(B.8) G⁡(t,Xt)=G⁡(s,Xs)+∫st∂rG⁡(r,Xr)​⁡𝑑r+∫st∑i=1d∂iG⁡(r,Xr)​⁡d​Xri.G(t,X_{t})=G(s,X_{s})+\int_{s}^{t}\partial_{r}G(r,X_{r})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r+\int_{s}^{t}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}G(r,X_{r})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i}.
Proof.

By construction, almost-surely, [s,T]∋t↦G⁡(t,Xt)[s,T]\ni t\mapsto G(t,X_{t}) is a piecewise absolutely continuous function in tt, so, almost-surely, its distributional derivative is a sum of an integrable function on [s,T][s,T] and finitely many atoms at s≤rj≤ts\leq r_{j}\leq t. The integrable function part is ∫st∂rG⁡(r,Xr)​⁡𝑑r\int_{s}^{t}\partial_{r}G(r,X_{r})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r, while for the jump part we note that at each jump time rjr_{j} the distributional derivative is is equal to ∂iG⁡(rj,Xrj)\partial_{i}G(r_{j},X_{r_{j}}), where ii corresponds to the coordinate that jumped at time rjr_{j}. Thus, we can decompose the sum over jumps to a double sum, one over i∈[d]i\in[d] and one over jumps at which the iith coordinate jumped, and then use the definition (B.7) to conclude the result. ∎

The next result tells us how to convert stochastic integrals to deterministic integrals.

Lemma B.2.

Let (Ht)t∈[0,T]=(Ht1,…,Htd)t∈[0,T](H_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}=(H_{t}^{1},\ldots,H_{t}^{d})_{t\in[0,T]} be a nonnegative dd-dimensional predictable process. Then, for any 0≤s≤t≤T0\leq s\leq t\leq T,

(B.9) 𝔼[∫stHr⋅dXr]=𝔼[∫stHr⋅λrdr].\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}H_{r}\cdot\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}H_{r}\cdot\lambda_{r}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\right].
Proof.

By summing over i∈[d]i\in[d] Equation (B.9) is an immediate consequence of Lemma 4.1 in [21]. ∎

As a consequence of Lemma B.1 and Lemma B.2 we get the following result.

Corollary B.3.

Let G:ℕd→ℝ≥0G:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a nonnegative function. Then,

(B.10) 𝔼⁡[G⁡(Xt)|Xs=xs]−G⁡(xs)=∑i=1d∫st𝔼⁡[∂iG⁡(Xr)​λri|Xs=xs]​⁡𝑑r.\mathbb{E}[G(X_{t})|X_{s}=x_{s}]-G(x_{s})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\int_{s}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\partial_{i}G(X_{r})\lambda^{i}_{r}|X_{s}=x_{s}]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r.
Proof.

By Lemma B.1,

G⁡(Xt)=G⁡(Xs)+∫st∑i=1d∂iG⁡(Xr)​⁡d​Xri,\displaystyle G(X_{t})=G(X_{s})+\int_{s}^{t}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}G(X_{r})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i},

so applying Lemma B.2 conditionally on Xs=xsX_{s}=x_{s} gives

𝔼⁡[G⁡(Xt)|Xs=xs]=G⁡(xs)+∑i=1d𝔼⁡[∫stG⁡(Xr+ei)​⁡d​Xri|Xs=xs]−∑i=1d𝔼⁡[∫stG⁡(Xr)​⁡d​Xri|Xs=xs]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[G(X_{t})|X_{s}=x_{s}]=G(x_{s})+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}G(X_{r}+e_{i})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i}\bigg|X_{s}=x_{s}\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}G(X_{r})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r}^{i}\bigg|X_{s}=x_{s}\right]
=G⁡(xs)+∑i=1d𝔼⁡[∫stG⁡(Xr+ei)​λri​⁡𝑑r|Xs=xs]−∑i=1d𝔼⁡[∫stG⁡(Xr)​λri​⁡𝑑r|Xs=xs]\displaystyle=G(x_{s})+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}G(X_{r}+e_{i})\lambda_{r}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\bigg|X_{s}=x_{s}\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}G(X_{r})\lambda_{r}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\bigg|X_{s}=x_{s}\right]
=G⁡(xs)+∑i=1d𝔼⁡[∫st∂iG⁡(Xr)​λri​⁡𝑑r|Xs=xs]=G⁡(xs)+∑i=1d∫st𝔼⁡[∂iG⁡(Xr)​λri|Xs=xs]​⁡𝑑r.\displaystyle=G(x_{s})+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{s}^{t}\partial_{i}G(X_{r})\lambda_{r}^{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\bigg|X_{s}=x_{s}\right]=G(x_{s})+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\int_{s}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\partial_{i}G(X_{r})\lambda_{r}^{i}|X_{s}=x_{s}]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r.

∎

Appendix C The Poisson-Föllmer process

In this section we construct the Poisson-Föllmer process using a simple extension of the one-dimensional construction due to [21]. In Appendix B we saw how standard Poisson processes can be modified using stochastic intensities to yield counting processes (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} as in Equation B.6. In this section we will choose the intensity (λt)t∈[0,T](\lambda_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} to depend on the process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}, which the intensity defines. This is analogous to the continuous setting where the drift and/or diffusion matrix depend on the value of the solution to the stochastic differential equation. The construction of such process goes through a fixed point argument.

Recall that we write the data distribution as

μ=f​πT,\mu=f\pi_{T},

with the assumption that ff is bounded from above and below by positive constants. Let

(C.1) h⁡(t,x)=PT−t​f​(x),h(t,x)=\mathrm{P}_{T-t}f(x),

and define the intensity λ=(λ1,…,λd):[0,T]×ℕd→ℝd\lambda=(\lambda^{1},\ldots,\lambda^{d}):[0,T]\times\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} by

(C.2) λi​(t,x):=h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x),i∈[d].\lambda^{i}(t,x):=\frac{h(t,x+e_{i})}{h(t,x)},\qquad i\in[d].

Let us derive some properties hh which will be useful later.

Lemma C.1.

Let h:ℕd→ℝh:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be as in Equation C.1. Then,

(C.3) ∂th(t,x)=−∑i=1d∂ih(t,x),\partial_{t}h(t,x)=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}h(t,x),
(C.4) ∂tlog⁡h⁡(t,x)=∑i=1d[1−h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x)]=∑i=1d[1−λi​(t,x)],\partial_{t}\log h(t,x)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[1-\frac{h(t,x+e_{i})}{h(t,x)}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[1-\lambda^{i}(t,x)\right],

and

(C.5) h⁡(T,x)=f⁡(x),h⁡(0,0)=1.h(T,x)=f(x),\qquad h(0,0)=1.
Proof.

Equation in (C.3) follows immediately from (A.11). Equation (C.4) follows from

∂tlogh(t,x)=∂th⁡(t,x)h⁡(t,x)=(C.3)−∑i=1d∂ih⁡(t,x)h⁡(t,x)=−∑i=1d[h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x)−1]=(C.2)∑i=1d[1−λi(t,x)].\displaystyle\partial_{t}\log h(t,x)=\frac{\partial_{t}h(t,x)}{h(t,x)}\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:h_pde]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:h_pde}\/)}}}}{=}-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{\partial_{i}h(t,x)}{h(t,x)}=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\frac{h(t,x+e_{i})}{h(t,x)}-1\right]\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:stoch_int_appen]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:stoch_int_appen}\/)}}}}{=}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[1-\lambda^{i}(t,x)\right].

Equation (C.5) follows from

h⁡(0,0)=PT​f​(0)=∑y∈ℕdf⁡(y)​πT​(y)=∑y∈ℕdμ⁡(y)=1.h(0,0)=\mathrm{P}_{T}f(0)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}f(y)\pi_{T}(y)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\mu(y)=1.

∎

We now turn to the existence of the Poisson-Föllmer process.

Lemma C.2 (Existence of the Poisson-Föllmer process).

There exists a counting process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} defined via Equation B.6 with λti:=λi​(t,Xt)\lambda^{i}_{t}:=\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t}) where λi​(t,x)\lambda^{i}(t,x) is as in Equation C.2 for i∈[d]i\in[d].

Proof.

We follow the proof of Lemma 4.3 in [21]. To avoid confusion set Gi​(t,x):=λi​(t,x)=h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x)G^{i}(t,x):=\lambda^{i}(t,x)=\frac{h(t,x+e_{i})}{h(t,x)} and let G:=(G1,…,Gd)G:=(G^{1},\ldots,G^{d}). Given a predictable intensity (λt)t∈[0,T](\lambda_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} let (Xt,λ)t∈[0,T](X_{t,\lambda})_{t\in[0,T]} denote the process defined via (B.6). Let ℋ:(λt)t∈[0,T]↦(G⁡(t,Xt,λ))t∈[0,T]\mathcal{H}:(\lambda_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\mapsto(G(t,X_{t,\lambda}))_{t\in[0,T]} be a function from the set of predictable nonnegative processes to itself. The proof of the lemma will be complete if ℋ\mathcal{H} has a fixed point. To this end let λ,α\lambda,\alpha be two predictable nonnegative processes. Each of the coordinates of G⁡(t,x)G(t,x) is bounded from above and below by positive constants since ff is bounded from above and below by positive constants, and by the definition of hh. Hence,

(C.6) 𝔼[|G(t,Xt,λ)−G(t,Xt,α)|]≤cℙ[Xt,λ≠Xt,α],\mathbb{E}[|G(t,X_{t,\lambda})-G(t,X_{t,\alpha})|]\leq c\,\mathbb{P}[X_{t,\lambda}\neq X_{t,\alpha}],

for some constant c>0c>0, where |⋅||\cdot| is the L1L^{1}-norm. Since Xt,λ,Xt,αX_{t,\lambda},X_{t,\alpha} are both ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}-valued we have

(C.7) ℙ[Xt,λ≠Xt,α]≤𝔼[|Xt,λ−Xt,α|],\mathbb{P}[X_{t,\lambda}\neq X_{t,\alpha}]\leq\mathbb{E}[|X_{t,\lambda}-X_{t,\alpha}|],

because when Xt,λ≠Xt,αX_{t,\lambda}\neq X_{t,\alpha} the value of |Xt,λi−Xt,αi||X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i}|, for at least one coordinate, is at least 1. Fix i∈[d]i\in[d]. By Lemma B.2,

𝔼[1{Xt,λi≥Xt,αi}(Xt,λi−Xt,αi)]=𝔼[∫0t1{Xt,λi≥Xt,αi}dXr,λi−∫0t1{Xt,λi≥Xt,αi}dXr,αi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}\geq X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}(X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i})]=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}\geq X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r,\lambda}^{i}-\int_{0}^{t}1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}\geq X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}X_{r,\alpha}^{i}\right]

𝔼[1{Xt,λi<Xt,αi}(Xt,λi−Xt,αi)]≤𝔼[∫0t|λri−αri|dr].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}<X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}(X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i})]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}|\lambda_{r}^{i}-\alpha_{r}^{i}|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\right].

𝔼⁡[|Xt,λi−Xt,αi|]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[|X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i}|] =𝔼[1{Xt,λi≥Xt,αi}(Xt,λi−Xt,αi)]+𝔼[1{Xt,λi<Xt,αi}(Xt,λi−Xt,αi)]≤2𝔼[∫0t|λri−αri|dr],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}\geq X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}(X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i})\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[1_{\{X_{t,\lambda}^{i}<X_{t,\alpha}^{i}\}}(X_{t,\lambda}^{i}-X_{t,\alpha}^{i})\right]\leq 2\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}|\lambda_{r}^{i}-\alpha_{r}^{i}|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\right],

so it follows that

(C.8) 𝔼⁡[|Xt,λ−Xt,α|]≤2​𝔼​[∫0t|λr−αr|​⁡𝑑r].\mathbb{E}[|X_{t,\lambda}-X_{t,\alpha}|]\leq 2\,\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}|\lambda_{r}-\alpha_{r}|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r\right].

(C.10) d⁡(λ,α):=∫0Te−2​c​t​𝔼​[|λt−αt|]​⁡𝑑t.d(\lambda,\alpha):=\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2ct}\mathbb{E}[|\lambda_{t}-\alpha_{t}|]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

Then, by (C.9) and integration by parts,

so ℋ\mathcal{H} is 12\frac{1}{2}-Lipschitz with respect to dd. Since the space of predictable nonnegative processes with bounded L1L^{1} norm is complete with respect to dd, it follows that ℋ\mathcal{H} has a fixed point. ∎

Appendix D Kolmogorov equations of the Poisson-Föllmer process

The purpose of this section is to derive the forward and backward Kolmogorov equations of the Poisson-Föllmer process. These will have a number of important consequences for us. We begin with the forward equations.

Lemma D.1 (Kolmogorov forward equations).

The translation probabilities (pt|s)0≤s≤t≤T(p_{t|s})_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T} of (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} satisfy, for all xs≤xt∈ℕdx_{s}\leq x_{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

(D.1) ∂tpt|s​(xt|xs)=∑i=1d[h⁡(t,xt)h⁡(t,xt−ei)​pt|s​(xt−ei|xs)−h⁡(t,xt+ei)h⁡(t,xt)​pt|s​(xt|xs)]=∑i=1d[λi​(t,xt−ei)​pt|s​(xt−ei|xs)−λi​(t,xt)​pt|s​(xt|xs)],\begin{split}\partial_{t}p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})&=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\frac{h(t,x_{t})}{h(t,x_{t}-e_{i})}p_{t|s}(x_{t}-e_{i}|x_{s})-\frac{h(t,x_{t}+e_{i})}{h(t,x_{t})}p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})\right]\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\lambda^{i}(t,x_{t}-e_{i})p_{t|s}(x_{t}-e_{i}|x_{s})-\lambda^{i}(t,x_{t})p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})\right],\end{split}

and the solution of Equation D.1 is

(D.2) pt|s​(xt|xs)=1xs≤xt​h⁡(t,xt)h⁡(s,xs)​πt−s​(xt−xs),pt=s|s​(xt|xs)=δxs​(xt),xs≤xt∈ℕd.p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})=1_{x_{s}\leq x_{t}}\frac{h(t,x_{t})}{h(s,x_{s})}\pi_{t-s}(x_{t}-x_{s}),\qquad p_{t=s|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})=\delta_{x_{s}}(x_{t}),\qquad x_{s}\leq x_{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.
Proof.

Fix any L1​(πT)L^{1}(\pi_{T})-integrable function G:ℕd→ℝG:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}. The identity (B.10) can be written as

(D.3) ∑xt∈ℕdG⁡(xt)​pt|s​(xt|xs)−G⁡(xs)=∑i=1d∫st[∑xr∈ℕdG⁡(xr+ei)​h⁡(r,xr+ei)h⁡(r,xr)​pr|s​(xr|xs)−∑xr∈ℕdG⁡(xr)​h⁡(r,xr+ei)h⁡(r,xr)​pr|s​(xr|xs)]​⁡dr,\begin{split}&\sum_{x_{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x_{t})p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})-G(x_{s})=\\ &\sum_{i=1}^{d}\int_{s}^{t}\left[\sum_{x_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x_{r}+e^{i})\frac{h(r,x_{r}+e^{i})}{h(r,x_{r})}p_{r|s}(x_{r}|x_{s})-\sum_{x_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}G(x_{r})\frac{h(r,x_{r}+e^{i})}{h(r,x_{r})}p_{r|s}(x_{r}|x_{s})\right]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r,\end{split}

so taking G⁡(x)=1x=yG(x)=1_{x=y}, for a fixed y∈ℕdy\in\mathbb{N}^{d}, gives

(D.4) pt|s​(y|xs)−1y=xs=∑i=1d∫st[∑xr∈ℕdh⁡(r,y)h⁡(r,y−ei)​pr|s​(y−ei|xs)−∑xr∈ℕdh⁡(r,y+ei)h⁡(r,y)​pr|s​(y|xs)]​⁡dr.\begin{split}&p_{t|s}(y|x_{s})-1_{y=x_{s}}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\int_{s}^{t}\left[\sum_{x_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\frac{h(r,y)}{h(r,y-e^{i})}p_{r|s}(y-e^{i}|x_{s})-\sum_{x_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\frac{h(r,y+e^{i})}{h(r,y)}p_{r|s}(y|x_{s})\right]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}r.\end{split}

Differentiating (D.4) with respect to tt establishes (D.1), where we used (C.2).

To verify (D.2) fix s,xss,x_{s}, and for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T let

g⁡(t,x):=1xs≤x​h⁡(t,x)h⁡(s,xs)​πt−s​(x−xs).g(t,x):=1_{x_{s}\leq x}\frac{h(t,x)}{h(s,x_{s})}\pi_{t-s}(x-x_{s}).

By (A.7) and (C.3),

=1xs≤x​1h⁡(s,xs)​∑i=1d[h⁡(t,x)​πt−s​(x−xs−ei)−h⁡(t,x+ei)​πt−s​(x−xs)]\displaystyle=1_{x_{s}\leq x}\frac{1}{h(s,x_{s})}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[h(t,x)\pi_{t-s}(x-x_{s}-e^{i})-h(t,x+e^{i})\pi_{t-s}(x-x_{s})\right]
=1xs≤x​1h⁡(s,xs)​∑i=1d[h⁡(t,x)h⁡(t,x−ei)​h​(t,x−ei)​πt−s​(x−xs−ei)−h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x)​h​(t,x)​πt−s​(x−xs)]\displaystyle=1_{x_{s}\leq x}\frac{1}{h(s,x_{s})}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\frac{h(t,x)}{h(t,x-e^{i})}h(t,x-e^{i})\pi_{t-s}(x-x_{s}-e^{i})-\frac{h(t,x+e^{i})}{h(t,x)}h(t,x)\pi_{t-s}(x-x_{s})\right]
=∑i=1d[h⁡(t,x)h⁡(t,x−ei)​g​(t,x−ei)−h⁡(t,x+ei)h⁡(t,x)​g​(t,x)],\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[\frac{h(t,x)}{h(t,x-e^{i})}g(t,x-e^{i})-\frac{h(t,x+e^{i})}{h(t,x)}g(t,x)\right],

which is precisely (D.1). ∎

A corollary of the Kolmogorov forward equation is that we can find an explicit form for the time marginals of the Poisson-Föllmer process. In particular, note that the next result shows that at time TT the Poisson-Föllmer process follows the data distribution μ\mu.

Corollary D.2 (Time marginals).

The time marginals (pt)t∈[0,T](p_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} of (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} satisfy the equation

(D.5) ∂tpt(xt)=−∑i=1d∂i[λi(t,xt−ei)pt(xt−ei)],\begin{split}\partial_{t}p_{t}(x_{t})=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{i}[\lambda^{i}(t,x_{t}-e_{i})p_{t}(x_{t}-e_{i})],\end{split}

and the solution to Equation D.5 is

(D.6) pt​(xt)=h⁡(t,xt)​πt​(xt),xt∈ℕd.p_{t}(x_{t})=h(t,x_{t})\pi_{t}(x_{t}),\qquad x_{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.
Proof.

Since X0=0X_{0}=0 we have pt​(xt)=pt|0​(xt|0)p_{t}(x_{t})=p_{t|0}(x_{t}|0). Thus, (D.5)-(D.6) follow by plugging s=0s=0 into (D.1)-(D.2), respectively, and using (C.5). ∎

Next we turn to the Kolmogorov backward equations.

Lemma D.3 (Kolmogorov backward equations).

Fix t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and let G:ℕd→ℝG:\mathbb{N}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be an L1​(πT)L^{1}(\pi_{T})-integrable function. For s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t] and xs∈ℕdx_{s}\in\mathbb{N}^{d} set

G⁡(s,xs):=𝔼⁡[G⁡(Xt)|Xs=xs],G⁡(t,xt)=G⁡(xt).G(s,x_{s}):=\mathbb{E}[G(X_{t})|X_{s}=x_{s}],\qquad\qquad G(t,x_{t})=G(x_{t}).

Then,

(D.7) ∂sG(s,xs)=−∑i=1dh⁡(s,xs+ei)h⁡(s,xs)∂iG(s,xs)=−∑i=1dλi(s,xs)∂iG(s,xs),\partial_{s}G(s,x_{s})=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{h(s,x_{s}+e^{i})}{h(s,x_{s})}\partial_{i}G(s,x_{s})=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda^{i}(s,x_{s})\partial_{i}G(s,x_{s}),

and the solution of Equation D.7 is

(D.8) G⁡(s,xs)=PT−s​(G​h​(t,⋅))​(xs)h⁡(s,xs).G(s,x_{s})=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{T-s}(Gh(t,\cdot))(x_{s})}{h(s,x_{s})}.

(D.9) ∂spt|s(xt|xs)=−∑i=1dh⁡(s,xs+ei)h⁡(s,xs)∂ipt|s(xt|xs)=−∑i=1dλi(s,xs)∂ipt|s(xt|xs).\partial_{s}p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{h(s,x_{s}+e^{i})}{h(s,x_{s})}\partial_{i}p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s})=-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda^{i}(s,x_{s})\partial_{i}p_{t|s}(x_{t}|x_{s}).
Proof.

Let G~\tilde{G} be a solution of (D.7). Then, by (B.8),

Appendix E Proofs

In this section we prove Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 2.3.

E.1. Proof of Proposition 2.2

Property (a) follows from Corollary D.2 with t=Tt=T. The next lemma establishes property (b).

Lemma E.1 (Bridges of Poisson-Föllmer process).

Let (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} be the Poisson-Föllmer process. Then, Xt|XT∼BinomialXT,tTX_{t}|X_{T}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}_{X_{T},\frac{t}{T}}.

pt​(x)​=(D.6)​h​(t,x)​πt​(x),pT​(y)​=(D.6)−(C.5)​f​(y)​πT​(y),\displaystyle p_{t}(x)\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:time_marg]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:time_marg}\/)}}}}{=}h(t,x)\pi_{t}(x),\qquad p_{T}(y)\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:time_marg]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:time_marg}\/)}}}-\hyperref@@ii[eq:h_bd]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:h_bd}\/)}}}}{=}f(y)\pi_{T}(y),

so by Bayes’ rule

pt|T​(x|y)\displaystyle p_{t|T}(x|y) =pT|t​(y|x)​pt​(x)πT​(y)=f⁡(y)h⁡(t,x)​πT−t​(y−x)​h⁡(t,x)​πt​(x)f⁡(y)​πT​(y)=πT−t​(y−x)​πt​(x)πT​(y)\displaystyle=p_{T|t}(y|x)\frac{p_{t}(x)}{\pi_{T}(y)}=\frac{f(y)}{h(t,x)}\pi_{T-t}(y-x)\frac{h(t,x)\pi_{t}(x)}{f(y)\pi_{T}(y)}=\frac{\pi_{T-t}(y-x)\pi_{t}(x)}{\pi_{T}(y)}
=∏i=1d(yixi)​(tT)xi​(T−tT)yi−xi=Binomialy,tT⁡(x).\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{d}{y^{i}\choose x^{i}}\left(\frac{t}{T}\right)^{x^{i}}\left(\frac{T-t}{T}\right)^{y^{i}-x^{i}}=\operatorname{Binomial}_{y,\frac{t}{T}}(x).

∎

The next lemma establishes property (c).

Lemma E.2 (Relation between denoiser and rate).

Let (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} be the Poisson-Föllmer process. Then,

and compute

∑y∈ℕdf⁡(Xt+y)​yi​πT−t​(y)=∑y−i∈ℕd−1(∏j≠iπT−t​(yj))​∑yi∈ℕfx−i,y−i​(Xti+yi)​yi​e−(T−t)​(T−t)yiyi!\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}f(X_{t}+y)y^{i}\pi_{T-t}(y)=\sum_{y^{-i}\in\mathbb{N}^{d-1}}\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\pi_{T-t}(y^{j})\right)\sum_{y^{i}\in\mathbb{N}}f_{x^{-i},y^{-i}}(X_{t}^{i}+y^{i})y^{i}e^{-(T-t)}\frac{(T-t)^{y^{i}}}{y^{i}!}
=(T−t)​∑y−i∈ℕd−1(∏j≠iπT−t​(yj))​∑yi∈ℕfx−i,y−i​((Xti+1)+(yi−1))​e−(T−t)​(T−t)yi−1(yi−1)!\displaystyle=(T-t)\sum_{y^{-i}\in\mathbb{N}^{d-1}}\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\pi_{T-t}(y^{j})\right)\sum_{y^{i}\in\mathbb{N}}f_{x^{-i},y^{-i}}((X_{t}^{i}+1)+(y^{i}-1))e^{-(T-t)}\frac{(T-t)^{y^{i}-1}}{(y^{i}-1)!}
=(T−t)​∑y−i∈ℕd−1(∏j≠iπT−t​(yj))​PT−t​fx−i,y−i​(Xti+1)\displaystyle=(T-t)\sum_{y^{-i}\in\mathbb{N}^{d-1}}\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\pi_{T-t}(y^{j})\right)\mathrm{P}_{T-t}f_{x^{-i},y^{-i}}(X_{t}^{i}+1)
=(T−t)​∑y−i∈ℕd−1(∏j≠iπT−t​(yj))​∑yi∈ℕf⁡((,,,))​πT−t​(yi)\displaystyle=(T-t)\sum_{y^{-i}\in\mathbb{N}^{d-1}}\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\pi_{T-t}(y^{j})\right)\sum_{y^{i}\in\mathbb{N}}f((x^{-i}+y^{-i},X_{t}^{i}+y^{i}+1))\pi_{T-t}(y^{i})

E.2. Proof of Proposition 2.3

To simplify the notation we will prove the proposition for T=1T=1, but the proof for the general case is similar. We recall that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu on ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d} we have

(E.2) KL⁡(ν|μ):=∑x∈ℕdlog⁡(ν⁡(x)μ⁡(x))​ν​(x).\mathrm{KL}(\nu|\mu):=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\log\left(\frac{\nu(x)}{\mu(x)}\right)\nu(x).

The proof of Proposition 2.3 will follow from the following lemma.

Lemma E.3.

Let

(E.3) ℓ⁡(a):=∑i=1dai​log⁡ai,∇ℓ​(a):=(1+log⁡a1,…,1+log⁡ad),a∈ℕd,\ell(a):=\sum_{i=1}^{d}a^{i}\log a^{i},\qquad\nabla\ell(a):=(1+\log a^{1},\ldots,1+\log a^{d}),\qquad a\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

and

(E.4) Dℓ​(a,b):=ℓ⁡(a)−ℓ⁡(b)−∇ℓ​(b)⋅(a−b)=∑i=1d[ai​log⁡ai−ai​log⁡bi−ai+bi],a,b∈ℕd.\begin{split}\mathrm{D}_{\ell}(a,b)&:=\ell(a)-\ell(b)-\nabla\ell(b)\cdot(a-b)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[a^{i}\log a^{i}-a^{i}\log b^{i}-a^{i}+b^{i}\right],\qquad a,b\in\mathbb{N}^{d}.\end{split}

Then, for x∈ℕdx\in\mathbb{N}^{d},

(E.5) ∂tKL(pt|1(⋅|x)|pt)=∑y∈ℕdDℓ(x−y1−t,λ(t,y))Binomialx,t(y).\begin{split}&\partial_{t}\mathrm{KL}(p_{t|1}(\cdot|x)|p_{t})=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\mathrm{D}_{\ell}\left(\frac{x-y}{1-t},\lambda(t,y)\right)\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,t}(y).\end{split}

Let us prove Proposition 2.3 assuming Lemma E.3.

Proof of Proposition 2.3.

Since

(E.6) p0=δ0,p1=μ,p0|1(⋅|x)=Binomialx,0=δ0,p1|1(⋅|x)=Binomialx,1=δx,p_{0}=\delta_{0},\qquad p_{1}=\mu,\qquad p_{0|1}(\cdot|x)=\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,0}=\delta_{0},\qquad p_{1|1}(\cdot|x)=\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,1}=\delta_{x},

we get

−logμ(x)=KL(δx|μ)=(E.6)KL(p1|1(⋅|x)|p1)−KL(p0|1(⋅|x)|p0)=∫01∂tKL(pt|1(⋅|x)|pt)dt\displaystyle-\log\mu(x)=\mathrm{KL}(\delta_{x}|\mu)\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:bd_flowtrans]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:bd_flowtrans}\/)}}}}{=}\mathrm{KL}(p_{1|1}(\cdot|x)|p_{1})-\mathrm{KL}(p_{0|1}(\cdot|x)|p_{0})=\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{t}\mathrm{KL}(p_{t|1}(\cdot|x)|p_{t})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t
=(E.5)​∫01∑y∈ℕdDℓ​(x−y1−t,λ⁡(t,y))​Binomialx,t⁡(y)​⁡𝑑t.\displaystyle\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:dert_log_kl_ell_lem]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:dert_log_kl_ell_lem}\/)}}}}{=}\int_{0}^{1}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\mathrm{D}_{\ell}\left(\frac{x-y}{1-t},\lambda(t,y)\right)\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,t}(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t.

∎

The remainder of the section is dedicated to the proof of Lemma E.3. We begin with some useful identities for the Binomial distribution, Bx,t:=Binomialx,t\mathrm{B}_{x,t}:=\operatorname{Binomial}_{x,t}.

=(∏j≠iBxj,t​(yj))​xi​{(xi−1)!(yi−1)!​(xi−1−(yi−1))!​tyi−1​(1−t)xi−1−(yi−1)}\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{j\neq i}\mathrm{B}_{x^{j},t}(y^{j})\right)x^{i}\left\{\frac{(x^{i}-1)!}{(y^{i}-1)!(x^{i}-1-(y^{i}-1))!}t^{y^{i}-1}(1-t)^{x^{i}-1-(y^{i}-1)}\right\}

We now turn to the proof of Lemma E.3. By definition,

KL(pt|T(⋅|x)|pt)=∑y∈ℕd[logBx,t(y)−logpt(y)]Bx,t(y),\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(p_{t|T}(\cdot|x)|p_{t})=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\left[\log\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)-\log p_{t}(y)\right]\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y),

so

Claim E.5.
(E.11) ∑y∈ℕdlog⁡(Bx,t​(y)pt​(y))​∂tBx,t​(y)=∑i=1d∑y∈ℕd{log⁡(xi−yi1−t)​xi−yi1−t−xi−yi1−t​log⁡λi​(t,y)}​Bx,t​(y).\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\log\left(\frac{\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)}{p_{t}(y)}\right)\partial_{t}\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\left\{\log\left(\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}\right)\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}-\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}\log\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right\}\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y).

and thus

∑y∈ℕdlog⁡(Bx,t​(y)pt​(y))​∂tBx,t​(y)=∑i=1d∑y∈ℕd{log⁡(xi−yi1−t)​xi−yi1−t−xi−yi1−t​log⁡λi​(t,y)}​Bx,t​(y).\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\log\left(\frac{\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)}{p_{t}(y)}\right)\partial_{t}\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\left\{\log\left(\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}\right)\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}-\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}\log\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right\}\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y).

∎

We now turn to the second term in (E.10).

Claim E.6.
(E.13) ∑y∈ℕd[∂tlog⁡Bx,t​(y)−∂tlog⁡pt​(y)]​Bx,t​(y)=∑i=1d∑y∈ℕd[xi−yi1−t+λi​(t,y)]​Bx,t​(y).\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\left[\partial_{t}\log\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)-\partial_{t}\log p_{t}(y)\right]\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\left[\frac{x^{i}-y^{i}}{1-t}+\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right]\mathrm{B}_{x,t}(y).
Proof.

Since

∎

With Claim E.5 and Claim E.6 in hand Equation (E.10) reads

Appendix F Schrödinger bridges

In this section we explain how the Poisson-Föllmer process is a special case of a Schrödinger bridge. Let D⁡([0,T],ℕd)D([0,T];\mathbb{N}^{d}) be the space of functions from [0,T][0,T] to ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}, and let RR be the law of the standard dd-dimensional Poisson process on ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}. Given a probably measure Q≪RQ\ll R on D⁡([0,T],ℕd)D([0,T];\mathbb{N}^{d}) we denote the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between QQ and RR as

(F.1) KL⁡(Q|R):=∫D⁡([0,T],ℕd)log⁡(⁡d​Q⁡d​R)​⁡𝑑Q.\mathrm{KL}(Q|R):=\int_{D([0,T];\mathbb{N}^{d})}\log\left(\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}R}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q.

For t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] we let Rt,QtR_{t},Q_{t} be the marginals of the coordinate process at time tt with respect to R,QR,Q, respectively.

Definition F.1 (Schrödinger problem for Dirac source).

Let RR be the Poisson measure over D⁡([0,T],ℕd)D([0,T];\mathbb{N}^{d}) and let μ\mu be a distribution over ℕd\mathbb{N}^{d}. Solve

(F.2) minQ⁡KL⁡(Q|R)such thatQ0∼δ0,QT∼μ.\min_{Q}\,\mathrm{KL}(Q|R)\quad\textnormal{such that}\quad Q_{0}\sim\delta_{0},\quad Q_{T}\sim\mu.

The problem introduces in Definition F.1 is a special case of the Schrödinger problem. In the general problem the source measure need not be a point mass, but for our purpose of designing a simple recipe for denoising and sampling, the problem (F.2) is better suited. Our goal in this section is to show that the Poisson-Föllmer process (Xt)t∈[0,T](X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} is an optimal solution to the Schrödinger problem for Dirac source. The next result gives a sufficient condition for a measure QQ to be an optimal solution to (F.2).

Lemma F.2.

If QQ satisfies

(F.3) KL⁡(Q|R)=KL⁡(μ|πT),\mathrm{KL}(Q|R)=\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\pi_{T}),

then QQ is an optimal solution to (F.2).

Proof.

Since the TT-marginal under RR is πT\pi_{T}, the chain rule for entropy gives

(F.4) KL⁡(Q|R)=KL⁡(μ|πT)+∑x∈ℕdKL⁡(Qx|Rx)​⁡d​μ​(x),\mathrm{KL}(Q|R)=\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\pi_{T})+\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\mathrm{KL}(Q^{x}|R^{x})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x),

where RxR^{x} (res. QxQ^{x}) is the bridge of RR (res. QQ) starting at 00 and terminating at xx. The term KL⁡(μ|πT)\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\pi_{T}) is the same for any QQ satisfying Q0∼δ0,QT∼μQ_{0}\sim\delta_{0},Q_{T}\sim\mu, which completes the argument. ∎

Our next result shows that if QQ is the law of the Poisson-Föllmer process then it satisfies (F.3), and hence it is an optimal solution to the Schrödinger problem.

Lemma F.3.

The law QQ of the Poisson-Föllmer process satisfies

(F.5) KL⁡(Q|R)=∑i=1d∫0T𝔼⁡[λi​(t,Xt)​log⁡λi​(t,Xt)−λi​(t,Xt)+1]​⁡𝑑t=KL⁡(μ|πT).\mathrm{KL}(Q|R)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})\log\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})-\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})+1\right]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t=\mathrm{KL}(\mu|\pi_{T}).
Proof.

The first equality in (F.5) is a consequence of Girsanov’s theorem for jump processes, e.g. Equation (14) in [10], and Equation (B.9). To establish the second equality in (F.5) we will show that

(F.6) ∂tKL⁡(pt|πt)=∑i=1d𝔼⁡[λi​(t,Xt)​log⁡λi​(t,Xt)−λi​(t,Xt)+1].\partial_{t}\mathrm{KL}(p_{t}|\pi_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}[\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})\log\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})-\lambda^{i}(t,X_{t})+1].

Once (F.6) is established we can deduce the result since π0=p0=δ0\pi_{0}=p_{0}=\delta_{0} and pT=μp_{T}=\mu. To prove (F.6) we compute

∂tKL⁡(pt|πt)​=(D.6)​∂t∑y∈ℕd[log⁡h⁡(t,y)]​pt​(y)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathrm{KL}(p_{t}|\pi_{t})\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:time_marg]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:time_marg}\/)}}}}{=}\partial_{t}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}[\log h(t,y)]p_{t}(y)
=(C.4),(D.5)​∑y∈ℕd∑i=1d[1−λi​(t,y)]​pt​(y)−∑i=1d∑y∈ℕdlog⁡h⁡(t,y)​∂i[λi​(t,y−ei)​pt​(y−ei)]\displaystyle\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:h_log_pde]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:h_log_pde}\/)}}},\hyperref@@ii[eq:time_marg_eq]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:time_marg_eq}\/)}}}}{=}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[1-\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right]p_{t}(y)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\log h(t,y)\partial_{i}[\lambda^{i}(t,y-e_{i})p_{t}(y-e_{i})]
=(A.2)​∑y∈ℕd∑i=1d{1−λi​(t,y)+∂ilog⁡h⁡(t,y)​λi​(t,y)}​pt​(y)​=(C.2)​∑y∈ℕd∑i=1d{1−λi​(t,y)+[log⁡λi​(t,y)]​λi​(t,y)}​pt​(y).\displaystyle\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:sum_by_parts]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:sum_by_parts}\/)}}}}{=}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left\{1-\lambda^{i}(t,y)+\partial_{i}\log h(t,y)\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right\}p_{t}(y)\overset{\hyperref@@ii[eq:stoch_int_appen]{\textup{{(\ignorespaces\ref*{eq:stoch_int_appen}\/)}}}}{=}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{N}^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left\{1-\lambda^{i}(t,y)+[\log\lambda^{i}(t,y)]\lambda^{i}(t,y)\right\}p_{t}(y).

∎

Appendix G Time reversal

The purpose of this section is to explain how our constructions is related to time-reversal of discrete diffusion models. Define the forward process Z→t:=XT−t\vec{Z}_{t}:=X_{T-t} to be a Poisson bridge which starts at Z→0∼μ\vec{Z}_{0}\sim\mu and terminates at Z→T=0\vec{Z}_{T}=0. Then the Poisson-Föllmer process Xt=:Zt→X_{t}=:\reflectbox{$\vec{\reflectbox{$Z_{t}$}}$} is the reverse process obtained by the time-reversal of Z→t\vec{Z}_{t}. Hence, from the perspective of the time-reversal approach in discrete diffusions [27] our goal should be learn the discrete score [qt​(y)qt​(x)]y≠x\left[\frac{q_{t}(y)}{q_{t}(x)}\right]_{y\neq x}, where qtq_{t} is the distribution of Z→t\vec{Z}_{t}. Since the forward process (Z→t)(\vec{Z}_{t}) decreases in increments of 1 in each coordinate, its rate matrices (Q→t)(\vec{Q}_{t}) take the form

(G.1) Q→t​(x,y)=1y∈{x−e1,…,x−ed}​1d,y≠x,\vec{Q}_{t}(x,y)=1_{y\in\{x-e_{1},\ldots,x-e_{d}\}}\,\frac{1}{d},\qquad\qquad y\neq x,

so the rate matrices (Q→t)(\reflectbox{$\vec{\reflectbox{$Q$}}$}_{t}) of the reverse process (Zt→)(\reflectbox{$\vec{\reflectbox{$Z_{t}$}}$}) are

(G.2) Q→t​(x,x+ei)=1d​qt​(x+ei)qt​(x),Q→t​(x,y)=0​ for ​y∉{x,x+e1,…,x+ed}.\vec{Q}_{t}(x,x+e_{i})=\frac{1}{d}\frac{q_{t}(x+e_{i})}{q_{t}(x)},\qquad\qquad\vec{Q}_{t}(x,y)=0\textnormal{ for }y\notin\{x,x+e_{1},\ldots,x+e_{d}\}.

Since qt=pT−tq_{t}=p_{T-t}, Corollary D.2 shows that

(G.3) qt​(x+ei)qt​(x)=h⁡(T−t,x+ei)​πT−t​(x+ei)h⁡(T−t,x)​πT−t​(x)=T−txi+1​λi​(T−t,x).\frac{q_{t}(x+e_{i})}{q_{t}(x)}=\frac{h(T-t,x+e_{i})\pi_{T-t}(x+e_{i})}{h(T-t,x)\pi_{T-t}(x)}=\frac{T-t}{x^{i}+1}\lambda^{i}(T-t,x).

Thus, learning the intensity λ\lambda of the Poisson-Föllmer process is equivalent to learning the time-reversal of the forward process (Z→t)(\vec{Z}_{t}).

Appendix H Gaussian analogues: The Föllmer process

The continuous analogue of the Poisson-Föllmer process is the Föllmer process. To describe this process we write the data distribution as

(H.1) μ=f​γ0,T,\mu=f\gamma_{0,T},

where γx,t\gamma_{x,t} is the Gaussian with mean x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and covariance t​IdtI_{d} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The heat semigroup is acting on L1​(γT)L^{1}(\gamma_{T})-integrable functions G:ℝd→ℝG:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} by

(H.2) Ht​G​(x):=∫ℝdG⁡(x+t​y)​⁡d​γ0,1​(y),H_{t}G(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}G(x+\sqrt{t}y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\gamma_{0,1}(y),

and the analogue of the Doob hh-transform in the continuous setting is

(H.3) h⁡(t,x):=HT−t​f​(x).h(t,x):=H_{T-t}f(x).

The Föllmer process is the solution to the stochastic differential equation over t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T],

(H.4) ⁡d​Yt=∇log⁡HT−t​f​(Yt)​⁡d​t+⁡d​Bt,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Y_{t}=\nabla\log H_{T-t}f(Y_{t})\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t+\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}B_{t},

where (Bt)(B_{t}) is a standard Brownian motion in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Analogous to Corollary D.2, the time marginals (pt)t∈[0,T](p_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} of (Yt)t∈[0,T](Y_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} satisfy

(H.5) pt​(x)=h⁡(t,x)​γ0,t​(x),p_{t}(x)=h(t,x)\gamma_{0,t}(x),

so, in particular, YT∼μY_{T}\sim\mu. The drift ∇log⁡HT−t​f\nabla\log H_{T-t}f is the continuous analogue of the intensity λ\lambda, and satisfies a Tweedie’s formula

(H.6) ∇log⁡HT−t​f​(x)=m⁡(t,x)−xT−t,\nabla\log H_{T-t}f(x)=\frac{\mathrm{m}(t,x)-x}{T-t},

where

m⁡(t,x):=𝔼⁡[YT|Yt=x].\mathrm{m}(t,x):=\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}|Y_{t}=x].

Thus, the drift ∇log⁡HT−t​f\nabla\log H_{T-t}f can be learned via objectives such as (1.3). To verify (H.6) we use the fact (Lemma 4.1 in [30]) that the distribution of YT|YtY_{T}|Y_{t} is y↦f⁡(y)​γYt,T−t​(y)HT−t​f​(Yt)y\mapsto\frac{f(y)\gamma_{Y_{t},T-t}(y)}{H_{T-t}f(Y_{t})}, so

𝔼⁡[YT|Yt]=∫ℝdy​f⁡(y)​γYt,T−t​(y)HT−t​f​(Yt)​⁡𝑑y,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}|Y_{t}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}y\frac{f(y)\gamma_{Y_{t},T-t}(y)}{H_{T-t}f(Y_{t})}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}y,

while on the other hand, by integration by parts,

∇log⁡HT−t​f​(x)=1HT−t​f​(x)​∫ℝd1T−t​∇yf​(x+T−t​y)​⁡d​γ0,1​(y)\displaystyle\nabla\log H_{T-t}f(x)=\frac{1}{H_{T-t}f(x)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{T-t}}\nabla_{y}f(x+\sqrt{T-t}y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\gamma_{0,1}(y)
=1HT−t​f​(x)​∫ℝdy​1T−t​f​(x+T−t​y)​⁡d​γ0,1​(y)=1T−t​∫ℝd(y−x)​f⁡(y)​⁡d​γx,T−t​(y)HT−t​f​(x).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{H_{T-t}f(x)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}y\frac{1}{\sqrt{T-t}}f(x+\sqrt{T-t}y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\gamma_{0,1}(y)=\frac{1}{T-t}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(y-x)\frac{f(y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\gamma_{x,T-t}(y)}{H_{T-t}f(x)}.

Note that, by (H.5) and (H.3),

(H.7) ∇log⁡pt​(x)=∇log⁡HT−t​f​(x)−xt=1T−t​m​(t,x)−Tt⁡(T−t)​x.\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\nabla\log H_{T-t}f(x)-\frac{x}{t}=\frac{1}{T-t}\mathrm{m}(t,x)-\frac{T}{t(T-t)}x.

Just like the Poisson-Föllmer process, the Föllmer process is a special case of a Schrödinger bridge, and the drift ∇log⁡HT−t​f\nabla\log H_{T-t}f is, up to a time change, the score one needs to learn in the time reversal of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.

Appendix I Experiments with synthetic data

In this section we define the one-dimensional synthetic distributions considered in Section 3, and provide additional details for training the denoiser with data from these problems. The synthetic experiments consist of the following distributions taken from [4], which all have a truncated support of integers 𝒪⊂ℕ01\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{N}_{0}^{1}, where the support size |𝒪||\mathcal{O}| is reported below for each problem.

  1. (1)

    Poisson Mixture: μ⁡(x)=∑i=1mwi​Poissonλi⁡(x)\mu(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}\operatorname{Poisson}_{\lambda_{i}}(x). We take m=2m=2 components with w1=0.1,w2=0.9w_{1}=0.1,w_{2}=0.9, λ1=1,λ2=100\lambda_{1}=1,\lambda_{2}=100 and |𝒪|=140|\mathcal{O}|=140.

    Zero-Inflated-Poisson (ZIP): μ⁡(x)=w0+(1−w0)​e−λ\mu(x)=w_{0}+(1-w_{0})e^{-\lambda} for x=0x=0 and μ⁡(x)=(1−w0)​Poissonλ⁡(x)\mu(x)=(1-w_{0})\operatorname{Poisson}_{\lambda}(x) for x>0x>0. We take w0=0.7w_{0}=0.7, λ=5\lambda=5, and |𝒪|=50|\mathcal{O}|=50.

    Negative-Binomial-Mixture (NBM): μ⁡(x)=∑i=1mwi​NegativeBinomialri,pi⁡(x)\mu(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}\operatorname{NegativeBinomial}_{r_{i},p_{i}}(x) where rir_{i} are the number of successes and pip_{i} are the success probabilities. We take m=2m=2 components with r1=1,r2=10r_{1}=1,r_{2}=10, p1=0.9,p2=0.1p_{1}=0.9,p_{2}=0.1, and |𝒪|=150|\mathcal{O}|=150.

  5. (5)

    Beta-Negative-Binomial (BNB): μ⁡(x)=∫01NegativeBinomial1,t⁡(x)​Betaa,b​(t)​⁡𝑑t\mu(x)=\int_{0}^{1}\operatorname{NegativeBinomial}_{1,t}(x)\text{Beta}_{a,b}(t)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t where Betaa,b​(t)\text{Beta}_{a,b}(t) is a Beta distribution with parameters a,ba,b. We take a=1.5,b=1.5a=1.5,b=1.5 and r=5r=5, and |𝒪|=100|\mathcal{O}|=100.

  6. (6)

    Zipf: μ⁡(x)=x−α/ζ⁡(α)\mu(x)=x^{-\alpha}/\zeta(\alpha) where ζ⁡(α)\zeta(\alpha) is Riemann zeta function. We take α=1.7\alpha=1.7 and |𝒪|=50|\mathcal{O}|=50.

  7. (7)

    Yule-Simon: μ⁡(x)=ρ​Γ​(x)​Γ​(ρ+1)/Γ⁡(x+ρ+1),\mu(x)=\rho\Gamma(x)\Gamma(\rho+1)/\Gamma(x+\rho+1), where Γ\Gamma is the Gamma function and ρ∈ℝ+\rho\in\mathbb{R}_{+} is a positive constant. We take ρ=2.0\rho=2.0 and |𝒪|=50|\mathcal{O}|=50.

For these experiments we use a residual MLP architecture for the denoiser with sinusoidal time-embeddings. The model has 3 hidden layers with 256 hidden dimensions, and 128 dimensional embeddings for time. We learn the network parameters using the Adam optimizer by training for 300300 epochs with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, a batch size of 128128, weight decay of magnitude 10−510^{-5}, gradient clipping, and taking an exponential moving average of the parameters for the reported results.

Figure 6 plots the log-likelihood of the predicted distribution over the support of the target distribution using identity (2.10), in comparison to the true log of the probability mass function (PMF) log⁡μ⁡(x)\log\mu(x). The predicted log-likelihood is computed using a Monte Carlo estimator with 10,00010,000 samples. The mean and standard error of the estimator are reported using the solid and dashed lines, respectively. We note that the estimated log-likelihood shows close agreement to the true PMF, especially in regions where the target distribution has higher probability mass, e.g., we note that growth in the standard error for the Yule-Simon distribution for larger xx.

Appendix J Experiments with imaging data

J.1. Preconditioning

In this section we provide further details on preconditioning. We follow the EDM framework [18] where we write

(J.1) mθ​(xt,t)=cskip​(t)​xt+cout​(t)​Fθ​(xt~,t),x~t=cin​(t)​xt+sin.\mathrm{m}_{\theta}(x_{t},t)=c_{\textnormal{skip}}(t)x_{t}+c_{\textnormal{out}}(t)F_{\theta}(\widetilde{x_{t}},t),\qquad\qquad\widetilde{x}_{t}=c_{\text{in}}(t)x_{t}+s_{\text{in}}.

Following EDM’s optimality principles, we derive scaling functions cin​(t)c_{\text{in}}(t), cskip​(t)c_{\text{skip}}(t), cout​(t)c_{\text{out}}(t) and loss weight w2​(t)w^{2}(t) to satisfy three criteria: (i) cin​(t)c_{\text{in}}(t) normalizes network inputs x~t\widetilde{x}_{t} to unit variance (and additional centering via sins_{\text{in}} in our case), (ii) cskip​(t)c_{\text{skip}}(t) minimizes cout​(t)c_{\text{out}}(t) to prevent error amplification while cout​(t)c_{\text{out}}(t) ensures unit variance training targets, and (iii) w2​(t)w^{2}(t) maintains constant expected loss across time levels. Just for the purpose of this derivation we assume that the coordinates of X1∼μX_{1}\sim\mu are i.i.d. with mean μdata\mu_{\textnormal{data}} and variance σdata2\sigma^{2}_{\textnormal{data}}.

J.1.1. Binomial noise

In this section we derive the EDM scaling for the Binomial noise used in our Binomial flow algorithm.
